sw_002:n1.prompt:
You are helping me draft the changelog for our next release as part of our "Cut a release" ritual. We host our code on {{vendor}}. If you don't already know it, ask me for: the repository name/path, the last release tag (or how to find it), and the target branch for this release.

Please do the following:
1. Using our configured credentials, connect to {{vendor}} and collect all pull/merge requests that have been merged into the target branch since the last release tag.
2. For each merged PR, extract the title, author, PR number/link, and any labels (e.g., bugfix, feature, breaking-change) if available.
3. Group the changes into clear sections (e.g., Features, Fixes, Breaking Changes, Chores) based on labels or commit conventions; if {{vendor}} offers AI-generated summaries or insights on the PRs, use them to help write concise, human-readable bullet descriptions for each change.
4. Flag anything ambiguous — PRs with unclear titles, missing labels, or potential breaking changes — in a separate "needs review" list.
5. Compile everything into a single draft changelog document (Markdown), with a clear heading for the proposed version/date and sections as above.

Done looks like: a complete draft changelog covering every merged PR since the last tag, organized into sections, with a short "needs review" list of ambiguous items, ready for a human to review before tagging.

Report back with: the draft changelog text, the count of PRs included, the list of flagged/ambiguous items, and the last tag/commit range used so I can verify completeness. Do not tag, publish, or approve the release — this step only prepares the draft changelog for the approval gate that follows.

sw_002:n2.prompt:
You are helping me tag a release in {{vendor}} (our code-hosting platform) as part of our release ritual. This step requires a human to explicitly approve the tag creation before it happens — you must prepare everything but not create or push the tag yourself.

First, ask me for anything you need that isn't already clear: the {{vendor}} repository name/URL, the target branch or commit SHA to tag, the version number/tag name to use (e.g. following semver), and where the changelog draft for this release lives (or ask me to paste it if it's not committed yet).

Then, using my configured credentials and {{vendor}}'s documented API or dashboard:
1. Confirm the target commit exists and pull its recent commit history/merged PR list so I can sanity-check what's included in this release.
2. Draft the exact tag name, target commit SHA, and annotation/message (incorporating the changelog summary) as a ready-to-apply proposal.
3. If {{vendor}} supports a change-approval workflow (e.g. required reviewers or protected tag rules) for this repo, check whether one is configured and note its status.
4. Present me a clear summary: repo, branch/commit, proposed tag name, tag message, and any approval workflow status.

Do not create, push, or apply the tag. Do not approve or bypass any approval workflow on my behalf. Once the proposal is ready, stop for human sign-off and tell me exactly what you prepared and what action I need to take (e.g. "approve and create the tag via {{vendor}}") to proceed.

Report back with: the repo/commit/tag details you prepared, any commit/PR list you reviewed, the approval workflow status you found, and a clear statement that you are stopping for human sign-off before the tag is created.

sw_002:n3.prompt:
You are helping me publish release notes for a software release as part of our repo's release ritual on {{vendor}}. Before starting, ask me for anything you need that isn't already available in your configured credentials or repo context: the repository name/URL, the release tag or version number that was just approved and tagged, and the draft changelog content (or confirm you should assemble it from merged PRs since the last release).

Steps to perform:
1. Using {{vendor}}'s API or dashboard, retrieve the list of merged pull requests since the last published release tag, and compile them into a clean, human-readable changelog grouped by type (features, fixes, chores, etc.) if labels/metadata support that grouping.
2. Create the release notes entry on {{vendor}} for the specified tag, using the compiled changelog as the body. Include the version, date, and a link to the full commit comparison if {{vendor}} supports that.
3. Publish the release notes so they are visible on the repository's releases page.
4. If {{vendor}} supports webhook-driven or chat-tool notifications, confirm that publishing this release will trigger the existing notification integration (e.g., a repo activity sync to a chat channel) — do not set up a new integration, just confirm the existing one will fire.
5. Do not tag, approve, or merge anything as part of this step — only publish the notes for a release that has already been tagged and approved.

When done, report back to me with: the release tag/version, a link to the published release notes, a summary of the changelog content included, and confirmation of whether the notification integration fired or is expected to fire. If you hit any ambiguity (e.g., missing PR labels, unclear grouping, or unclear tag target), stop and ask me rather than guessing.

sw_002:n4.prompt:
You are helping me monitor errors after a production release using {{vendor}}, our error-tracking tool. This is an async step: results (error counts, affected users) will accumulate over the next 30-60 minutes, so you must poll {{vendor}} periodically rather than expect instant results, and clearly report when you've verified a stable read.

First, ask me for anything you don't already have: our domain/app name, the release version or git tag we just shipped, the {{vendor}} project identifier/slug, the target environment (e.g. production), and where alerts should route (Slack channel, PagerDuty service, or email) if not already configured.

Then: using {{vendor}}'s error-search API or MCP tool, pull the top issues tied to this release, including stack traces, affected-user/session counts, and whether each is new, a regression of a previously resolved issue, or an existing known issue. Prioritize by blast radius (users/sessions affected), not raw event volume. Check release health metrics — crash-free sessions/users and adoption — and compare this release against the last stable one if that view is available. Flag any regressions (issues marked resolved that reappeared in this release) distinctly from new issues.

For issues that look like real bugs (not noise), draft ticket entries (title, stack trace, affected-user count, suspect commit if shown) ready to file into our tracker, but don't file them yet — list them for me to confirm first.

Report back: a summary of top issues by impact, crash-free rate vs. baseline, any regressions detected, draft tickets prepared, and your recommendation on whether this release looks healthy or warrants a rollback. Note the timestamp of your last poll and whether you consider monitoring still in progress or concluded.

sw_002:n5.prompt:
You are helping me prepare a rollback decision package for a release we just shipped, as part of our 'Cut a release' ritual. This is a judgment call I must make myself — you are only assembling the information and readiness materials, not deciding or executing the rollback.

Please do the following:

1. Ask me for: the repository/project name, the release tag or version just deployed, and where our post-deploy error/health signals live (e.g. our error tracker, logs dashboard, or monitoring tool) if not already known from context.
2. Using my configured credentials, pull the current error rates, key health metrics, and any alerts triggered since this release went live. Compare them to the pre-release baseline if available.
3. Summarize what changed in this release (from the changelog or merged PRs) so I can see what's plausibly related to any anomalies.
4. Draft a clear rollback decision brief containing: current signal summary, severity assessment (what's degraded, how much, how many users/requests affected), the specific rollback steps our CI/CD pipeline would run if I approve, and estimated time/impact of rolling back versus staying forward.
5. Prepare, but do not trigger, the rollback command or pipeline job — have it staged and ready to run only after my explicit go-ahead.

Do not decide whether a rollback is warranted, and do not initiate, approve, or execute the rollback yourself. This decision is a policy gate that only I can make. Once the brief and staged rollback steps are ready, stop for human sign-off and present me with the summary, the evidence, and the exact staged action awaiting my approval.
